messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 42

He is seventy-nine now, a wiry African man who still works part-time in a warehouse because, as he puts it, “moving boxes is easier than sitting with my mind.” He arrives on time, polite and composed, with the steady habits of someone who has spent a lifetime making himself useful. It takes several meetings before he begins to talk about the house where he grew up, and the sounds that still live with him.

As a boy, he shares a small home with his parents and siblings. At night, after the cooking fire dies down and the neighborhood quiets, he learns to listen for changes in his father’s footsteps. He can tell, even before the door opens, whether his father has come home calm or angry. On the bad nights, he hears his mother’s voice drop into a pleading tone and then the sudden crash of a chair, a pot, a body against the wall. He remembers staying very still on his sleeping mat, heart pounding so hard he is sure everyone can hear it. Sometimes his younger siblings press against him, and he feels he has to be the one who keeps them silent. He wants to run into the room and stop it; he also knows he is small and his father is not. That helplessness settles into him early, heavy as a stone.

One night stands out more sharply than the others. He is still a child, but old enough to understand fear in a permanent way. He sees his father strike his mother until she falls, then continue while she tries to shield her head. He remembers the sound more than the sight: breath knocked out of her, dishes breaking, his siblings crying. He does not move. Later, that becomes the part he cannot forgive in himself, though he knows he had no real power. In the morning, everyone behaves as if nothing happened. His mother cooks. His father speaks normally. The silence around the violence teaches him another lesson: what is terrible can also be ordinary.

He leaves home young and works wherever he can. Labor suits him. In warehouses, markets, loading docks, there is always something to lift, sort, stack, repair. He likes the clarity of tasks and the relief of exhaustion. He marries, has children, and tries to be the opposite of his father—quiet, restrained, never raising a hand. But anger in other people unnerves him. If his wife speaks sharply during an argument, his chest tightens and his thoughts scatter. He becomes withdrawn rather than confrontational, leaving the room, taking long walks, staying late at work. His marriage eventually ends in divorce. He does not describe dramatic fights; instead he talks about distance, his habit of shutting down, and how hard it has always been for him to remain present when voices rise.

Over the years he sleeps lightly. He wakes before dawn, alert in an instant, as if summoned by danger. He has dreams in which he is back in the house of his childhood, unable to reach his mother, his legs heavy and useless. Loud noises—metal clanging, something dropped suddenly behind him—send a jolt through him before he can think. At the warehouse, when pallets slam or two coworkers begin arguing near the loading bay, he feels sweat gather under his shirt. He scans the room automatically, locating exits, judging who is bigger, who might lose control. Sometimes he snaps at younger workers to “keep it down,” then feels embarrassed by the force in his own voice.

He avoids certain things without realizing at first that he is avoiding them. He does not watch films with scenes of family conflict. He changes the subject when relatives talk about “strict fathers” as if it were a joke. He has spent decades telling himself that other people had it worse, that he was never the one being hit. Yet his body does not believe those arguments. Even now, if he hears a woman crying through an apartment wall or from a passing open window, he goes rigid. He feels again like the boy on the mat, listening, waiting, ashamed.

What troubles him most in the present is not only the memories but the way they have shaped his whole life. He says he has been “on guard for so long it feels like my natural posture.” He keeps busy, keeps his room orderly, keeps his feelings narrowed into manageable channels. Still, there are moments when the past comes close: when a supervisor raises his voice, when a couple argues on the street, when he wakes from a dream with his fists clenched. In those moments he is no longer an old man stacking inventory and checking shipments. He is a child again, braced for the next sound from the next room, trying to make himself small enough to survive it.
